items.title: Look Out Circular in India: Travel Ban and Remedies
items.seoTitle: Look Out Circular in India: Travel Ban and Remedies
items.description: Look out circular in India: who can issue it, grounds, effect at the airport, how to challenge it in the High Court and travel permission in criminal cases.
items.html:
A look out circular (LOC) is an instruction issued to the immigration authorities to stop a person from leaving India, or to alert the agency that wants to track his movements. Many people discover it only at the airport, when they are stopped at the immigration counter. This guide explains who can issue a look out circular, the grounds, how to find out if one exists and how to challenge it.

What is a look out circular?

An LOC is issued by the Bureau of Immigration on the request of an originating agency, under guidelines issued by the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) in an Office Memorandum of 2010 that has been revised several times. It is an executive measure, and not an order of conviction. It does not require the person to be informed beforehand.

Who can request an LOC?

The guidelines list authorities such as the police, the CBI, the Enforcement Directorate, the Directorate of Revenue Intelligence, the Income Tax Department, the NIA, courts, and, in specified situations, heads of public sector banks. The request must be made in a prescribed format with details of the person and the case.

Grounds for issuing an LOC

The guidelines are meant to cover situations where a person is accused of a cognizable offence and is deliberately evading arrest or not appearing before the court, and cases where the departure of the person is considered detrimental to the sovereignty, security or integrity of India or the economic interest of the country. The High Courts have said that an LOC should not be issued as a routine step or merely to pressure a person to cooperate with an investigation.

What happens at the airport?

The immigration officer checks the person's details in the system. If there is an LOC, the person is not allowed to leave. The officer may inform the originating agency, and the agency may question or detain the person if required. Even a person with a valid visa and a ticket can be stopped.

How to find out if an LOC exists

There is no public database. In practice, a person finds out when he is stopped, or by asking the agency or through a lawyer who can approach the Bureau of Immigration and the originating agency. If a case is pending against you, assume that the possibility exists and take legal advice before travelling.

How to challenge an LOC

  • Request the originating agency in writing to withdraw or modify the LOC, explaining that you will cooperate with the investigation and attend the court. Give details of your residence, family, business and willingness to give an undertaking.
  • Approach the High Court by writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution. The Delhi High Court in *Sumer Singh Salkan v. Assistant Director* (2010) held that an LOC should be limited to cases of cognizable offences where the accused is evading the process of law. Other High Courts have followed similar principles and have set aside LOCs issued without proper grounds or reasons.
  • Seek permission to travel from the trial court, where the person is on bail and the bail order has a condition about leaving the country. The Supreme Court allowed an accused to travel abroad subject to conditions in *Karti P. Chidambaram v. Enforcement Directorate* (2018).

The right to travel abroad is recognised as part of personal liberty under Article 21, as held in *Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India* (1978). Courts balance this right against the interest of the investigation and the trial.

Passport issues in criminal cases

Separately from an LOC, the Passports Act, 1967 allows the passport authority to refuse or impound a passport where criminal proceedings are pending, subject to the exceptions in the government notifications, which let the court permit the issue or renewal. Anyone with a pending case should check the effect on passport renewal and foreign travel.

Practical steps

  • Get a copy of the FIR and the bail order, and check whether any travel condition exists.
  • Prepare an undertaking to return and to appear before the court.
  • Keep records of your residence, family, employment and property in India.
  • Where a bank or a creditor is behind the LOC, understand the dispute and consider settlement or an application for the LOC to be withdrawn.
  • If an arrest is feared, consider anticipatory bail under BNSS Section 482 and know your rights from our guide on arrest and detention rights under BNSS. For bail conditions that restrict travel, see regular bail and default bail under BNSS.

The guidelines and notices are published on the websites of the Ministry of Home Affairs and the Bureau of Immigration.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is a look out circular?

It is an alert issued to immigration authorities, on the request of an investigating or other authorised agency, to prevent a person from leaving India or to track his movement.

Who issues an LOC?

The Bureau of Immigration issues it on the request of an originating agency such as the police, CBI, ED, courts or, in limited cases, public sector banks.

Will I be told before an LOC is issued?

Generally no. Many people find out at the airport.

Can a look out circular be cancelled?

Yes. The originating agency can withdraw it, and the High Court can quash it in a writ petition if it was issued without proper grounds.

Does an LOC mean I am guilty?

No. It is an executive measure to ensure presence for investigation or trial, not a finding of guilt.

Can I travel abroad if I am on bail?

Only if the bail conditions allow, or if the court gives permission. Courts often allow travel with conditions such as an undertaking to return or surety.

Is a lawyer needed to challenge an LOC?

A writ petition requires proper drafting and facts, and a lawyer can also approach the agency for withdrawal, so legal help is strongly advised.

This article is general legal information and not a substitute for advice on your specific case. Consult an advocate before acting.

items.title: Criminal Trial Procedure under BNSS: Stages, Timelines
items.seoTitle: Criminal Trial Procedure under BNSS: Stages, Timelines
items.description: Criminal trial procedure under BNSS: charge sheet, cognizance, supply of documents, discharge, charge, evidence, arguments, judgment and key timelines.
items.html:
Criminal trial procedure under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) is the sequence of steps through which a criminal case moves from the filing of the police report to the final judgment. The BNSS keeps the structure of the old Code of Criminal Procedure but adds timelines at several stages and allows the use of electronic modes. This guide explains the stages in a simple order.

Types of criminal trial procedure

The procedure depends on the seriousness of the offence.

  • Sessions trial: For serious offences triable by the Court of Session, such as murder. The Magistrate commits the case to the Sessions Court.
  • Warrant case: For offences punishable with death, life imprisonment or imprisonment above two years, tried by a Magistrate.
  • Summons case: For less serious offences punishable up to two years, with a simpler procedure.
  • Summary trial: For minor offences, which is a quick procedure.

Stage 1: Investigation and charge sheet

After the FIR is registered, the police investigate and file a final report (charge sheet) before the Magistrate. For how an FIR starts the process, read our guide on FIR registration under BNSS Section 173. If the accused was arrested, the rules of custody and default bail govern the period of detention.

Stage 2: Cognizance and supply of documents

The Magistrate takes cognizance of the offence. Under Section 230 BNSS, copies of the police report, the FIR, statements and documents must be supplied to the accused, and to the victim if represented by an advocate, free of cost, within fourteen days of the accused's appearance or production.

Stage 3: Commitment, if the case is triable by Sessions

Where the offence is triable only by the Court of Session, the Magistrate commits the case to that court under Section 232.

Stage 4: Discharge

The accused can ask the court to discharge him if the material on record does not make out a case.

  • In a Sessions case, the application must be filed within sixty days from the date of commitment (Section 250).
  • In a warrant case on a police report, the period is sixty days from the supply of documents (Section 262).

The court hears both sides, and if it finds no sufficient ground for proceeding, it discharges the accused and records reasons. If not, it proceeds to frame the charge.

Stage 5: Framing of charge

The court frames a charge stating the offence. In a Sessions case, the charge should be framed within sixty days from the first hearing on charge (Section 251). The charge is read and explained to the accused, who is asked whether he pleads guilty or claims trial. A guilty plea may be accepted, subject to the court's satisfaction. For an alternative route to an early sentence, read our guide on plea bargaining under BNSS.

Stage 6: Prosecution evidence

The prosecution examines its witnesses. Each witness is subject to examination-in-chief, cross-examination and re-examination. Documents and material objects are marked as exhibits. The BNSS allows evidence to be recorded through audio-video electronic means and permits the use of electronic mode for proceedings.

Stage 7: Statement of the accused

After the prosecution evidence is complete, the court puts the incriminating circumstances to the accused and records his answers. The accused is not sworn, and he may choose to explain or deny.

Stage 8: Defence evidence

If the court does not acquit at this stage, the accused may lead evidence. He may examine himself or other witnesses and produce documents.

Stage 9: Arguments and judgment

The prosecution and defence argue. Under Section 258 BNSS, the judgment should be pronounced within thirty days of the completion of arguments, extendable up to forty-five days for reasons recorded in writing. These timelines are directory in nature in practice, but they signal the intention of the law.

Stage 10: Sentence and appeal

On a finding of guilt, the court hears the accused on the sentence. A convicted person, and in some cases the State or the victim, can file an appeal. For more, see our guide on criminal appeal and revision under BNSS.

Other features of the BNSS

  • Limits on adjournments, so that the trial is not delayed unnecessarily.
  • Trial in the absence of a proclaimed offender, subject to safeguards.
  • Audio-video recording of search and seizure.
  • Greater role for the victim in being informed and heard.

These details should be read from the Sanhita and updated rules. The text is on India Code.

Practical tips for the accused

  • Collect and study the documents supplied under Section 230 carefully.
  • Consider the discharge application within the time limit.
  • Keep track of every hearing date, since non-appearance can lead to a warrant.
  • Prepare for cross-examination, since it often decides the case.

Frequently Asked Questions

What are the stages of a criminal trial under BNSS?

Charge sheet, cognizance, supply of documents, commitment where needed, discharge, framing of charge, prosecution evidence, statement of the accused, defence evidence, arguments, judgment and sentence.

What is the time limit to file a discharge application?

In Sessions cases, sixty days from commitment under Section 250. In warrant cases on a police report, sixty days from supply of documents under Section 262.

When should the court frame the charge?

In a Sessions case, within sixty days from the first hearing on charge under Section 251.

Within what time should the judgment be pronounced?

Within thirty days of the completion of arguments, extendable to forty-five days with written reasons, under Section 258.

What is the difference between a sessions trial and a warrant case?

A sessions trial is for the most serious offences and is conducted by the Court of Session after commitment. A warrant case is tried by a Magistrate for offences punishable with more than two years.

Can the trial be held in electronic mode?

The BNSS allows evidence and proceedings to be conducted through electronic means in the manner allowed by law and the court.

Does the victim have a right in the trial?

Yes. The BNSS strengthens the rights of the victim to receive documents, to be heard at certain stages, and to be informed of the progress of the case.

This article is general legal information and not a substitute for advice on your specific case. Consult an advocate before acting.

items.title: NDPS Act Bail: Section 37 Twin Conditions and Remedies
items.seoTitle: NDPS Act Bail: Section 37 Twin Conditions and Remedies
items.description: NDPS Act bail explained: small, intermediate and commercial quantity, Section 37 twin conditions, procedural safeguards, charge sheet period and remedies.
items.html:
NDPS Act bail is harder to obtain than bail in ordinary offences because of the strict condition in Section 37 of the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985. The Act punishes possession, sale, transport and consumption of narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances, and the punishment depends on the quantity involved. This guide explains the classification, the twin conditions for bail and the safeguards that often decide NDPS cases.

Quantity and punishment

The Act and its notification classify each substance into three categories:

  • Small quantity: Punishment is generally imprisonment up to six months, or fine, or both. Bail is not subject to the special conditions of Section 37.
  • Intermediate quantity (more than small but less than commercial): Rigorous imprisonment up to ten years and a fine.
  • Commercial quantity: Rigorous imprisonment of not less than ten years, which may extend to twenty years, and a heavy fine. Section 37 applies.

Personal consumption of a drug is punishable under Section 27, and for small quantities the penalty is lighter. Financing illicit traffic is punishable under Section 27A and attracts Section 37.

NDPS Act bail: Section 37 twin conditions

For offences under Sections 19, 24 and 27A, and for offences involving commercial quantity, the Act says that a person accused of the offence shall not be released on bail unless:

  • The Public Prosecutor has been given an opportunity to oppose the application; and
  • The court is satisfied that there are reasonable grounds for believing that the accused is not guilty of the offence and that he is not likely to commit any offence while on bail.

These conditions apply in addition to the general rules on bail. Courts examine only the broad probabilities from the record, and not the detailed evidence, at the bail stage. The Supreme Court has held that Section 37 does not completely take away the power to grant bail, and that bail can be granted if the twin conditions are satisfied on the material. The classification of cases for bail in *Satender Kumar Antil v. CBI* (2022) places NDPS cases in a category that requires the stricter conditions.

Procedural safeguards that help the accused

NDPS cases frequently turn on whether the officers followed the mandatory procedure. Defence counsel examine the following:

  • Section 50 (personal search): If an officer is about to search a person, the person has the right to be taken to a gazetted officer or Magistrate. The Supreme Court has said compliance is mandatory, and the accused must be told of this right.
  • Section 42 and 43: Conditions for search and seizure without warrant, recording of information and sending a copy to the superior officer within the prescribed time.
  • Section 52A: Inventory, photography and sampling of the seized drug in the presence of a Magistrate. The Supreme Court has laid down that failure to follow the procedure can weaken the prosecution.
  • Chain of custody: Proof that the sample sent to the laboratory is the same as the substance seized, and that the seal was intact.
  • Independent witnesses: Whether independent witnesses were present at the recovery.
  • Statements to NDPS officers: In *Tofan Singh v. State of Tamil Nadu* (2020), the Supreme Court held that statements recorded by NDPS officers under Section 67 cannot be used as confessional statements against the accused in the trial.

Investigation period and default bail

Under Section 36A(4) of the Act, the period for filing the charge sheet in offences punishable with more than ten years is 180 days, and the Special Court can extend it up to one year on the report of the Public Prosecutor. Default bail rights depend on this special timeline, which is longer than the ordinary 60 or 90 days. For general principles of default bail, read our guide on regular bail and default bail under BNSS.

Long incarceration

Courts have recognised that where a trial is not likely to conclude within a reasonable time and the accused has spent a long period in custody, constitutional courts may grant bail despite Section 37, since the right to a speedy trial under Article 21 is also an important consideration. This depends on the facts of each case and the quantity involved.

Treatment for addicts

Section 64A gives immunity from prosecution to an addict who is charged with offences involving small quantity and who volunteers for medical treatment at a government-recognised centre, subject to conditions. Courts also consider rehabilitation in appropriate cases.

Where to apply for bail

Offences are tried by the Special Court under the Act. A bail application goes to that court. If it is refused, the High Court can be approached under Section 483 of the BNSS. The first step for a person who fears arrest is to consider anticipatory bail under BNSS Section 482. Know your rights at the time of arrest from our guide on arrest and detention rights under BNSS. The Act is available on India Code.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Section 37 of the NDPS Act?

It imposes twin conditions for bail in serious offences: the Public Prosecutor must be heard, and the court must be satisfied that there are reasonable grounds to believe that the accused is not guilty and is unlikely to commit an offence on bail.

Does Section 37 apply to every NDPS case?

No. It applies to offences under Sections 19, 24 and 27A and to offences involving commercial quantity. Small quantity cases are not subject to it.

What is commercial quantity?

It is the quantity notified by the government for each substance, above which the stricter punishment of ten to twenty years applies. The limits differ for each drug.

Why is Section 50 important?

It gives a person the right to be searched before a gazetted officer or Magistrate. Failure to inform the accused of this right can affect the prosecution case in a search of the person.

Are statements made to NDPS officers admissible?

In Tofan Singh v. State of Tamil Nadu, the Supreme Court held that statements made to NDPS officers under Section 67 are not admissible as confessions in the trial.

Can an addict avoid prosecution?

Under Section 64A, an addict who volunteers for treatment may get immunity for offences involving small quantity, subject to the conditions in the Act.

Is a lawyer necessary for NDPS bail?

Yes. The case depends on technical procedure, quantity classification and evidence, so early legal advice is essential.

This article is general legal information and not a substitute for advice on your specific case. Consult an advocate before acting.

items.title: Defamation under BNS Section 356: Offence and Defences
items.seoTitle: Defamation under BNS Section 356: Offence and Defences
items.description: Defamation under BNS Section 356: meaning, exceptions, punishment, how to file a complaint, online defamation, defences and civil damages explained.
items.html:
Defamation under BNS is the offence of harming a person's reputation by words, signs or visible representations, and it is dealt with in Section 356 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS), which replaced Sections 499 and 500 of the Indian Penal Code. The Supreme Court upheld criminal defamation as constitutional in *Subramanian Swamy v. Union of India* (2016), holding that the right to reputation is part of the right to life under Article 21. This guide explains the offence, the exceptions, the procedure and the practical points for complainants and accused persons.

What is defamation under BNS?

A person commits defamation if, by words (spoken or written), signs or visible representations, he makes or publishes an imputation concerning any person, intending to harm, or knowing or having reason to believe that it will harm, that person's reputation. The Sanhita also covers imputations made through electronic means, so social media posts, messages and videos can be covered.

Some points to remember:

  • The imputation must be published, which means communicated to someone other than the person defamed.
  • Harm to reputation is judged by how right-thinking people would view the person, not by the person's own hurt feelings.
  • An imputation about a deceased person, or about a company or a group of persons, can amount to defamation in certain conditions.

Punishment

The Sanhita provides for simple imprisonment up to two years, or fine, or both, or community service. Community service is a new form of punishment introduced by the BNS. Printing or engraving defamatory matter, and selling printed defamatory material, are separate offences with their own punishment.

Exceptions

The Sanhita lists exceptions under which an imputation is not defamation. The main ones are:

  • Imputation of truth for the public good, which is made or published for the public good.
  • Public conduct of public servants and opinions on their conduct made in good faith.
  • Conduct of any person touching a public question, expressed in good faith.
  • Publication of reports of court proceedings, if substantially true.
  • Merits of a case decided by a court, or the conduct of witnesses and parties, in good faith.
  • Merits of a public performance, such as a book or film review, in good faith.
  • Censure passed in good faith by a person having lawful authority over another.
  • Accusation made in good faith to an authorised person, such as a complaint to the police or an employer.
  • Imputation made in good faith for protecting one's own or another's interest.
  • Caution conveyed in good faith for the good of a person, or for the public good.

Good faith is the key. A statement made carelessly or with malice is not protected.

How to file a complaint

Defamation is a non-cognizable, bailable and compoundable offence in the usual scheme of the Code. The police cannot investigate without the Magistrate's order, so the aggrieved person files a private complaint before the Magistrate.

  • The complaint must set out the words, the date, the persons to whom it was published, and the harm caused.
  • The Magistrate records the complainant's sworn statement and may examine witnesses.
  • Under Section 223 of the BNSS, the Magistrate must give the accused an opportunity to be heard before taking cognizance of a complaint, which is a new safeguard.
  • If satisfied, the Magistrate issues summons, and the case is tried as a summons case.

Sending a legal notice first is not required by the criminal law, but it often helps to settle the matter or to prove the intention to resolve.

Online defamation

Posts on social media, WhatsApp groups, blogs and YouTube videos can be defamatory. Section 66A of the Information Technology Act was struck down in *Shreya Singhal v. Union of India* (2015), so complaints for online defamation proceed under the Sanhita. You can also ask the platform to remove content, and in cases involving obscene or morphed images, use the cybercrime reporting mechanisms. See our guide on cybercrime and online fraud under BNS and the IT Act. Always preserve screenshots with the URL, date and time, and the profile details.

Civil defamation

A person can also sue in a civil court for damages and a permanent injunction against the publication. Criminal and civil remedies can run together. For interim relief, see our guide on temporary injunction under Order 39 CPC.

Defending a defamation complaint

  • Check whether the statement was published, whether it identifies the complainant, and whether it was a statement of fact or opinion.
  • Rely on an exception, such as truth for the public good or good faith.
  • Challenge the complaint if it is vague, if the accused has no connection with the publication, or if it is an attempt to silence legitimate criticism.
  • Consider an apology or a settlement, since the offence is compoundable.
  • Where the allegations are plainly an abuse of process, a petition for quashing of FIR or proceedings under BNSS Section 528 may be possible.

The Sanhita is available on India Code.

Frequently Asked Questions

Which section of the BNS deals with defamation?

Section 356 of the BNS, which replaced Sections 499 and 500 of the Indian Penal Code. It defines the offence, lists the exceptions and prescribes the punishment.

What is the punishment for defamation?

Simple imprisonment up to two years, or fine, or both, or community service.

Is defamation a bailable offence?

Yes. It is bailable and non-cognizable, and it is compoundable, which means the parties can settle it.

Can I file an FIR for defamation?

Usually not. As it is a non-cognizable offence, you must file a complaint before the Magistrate, who will examine the matter and decide whether to issue summons.

Is truth a complete defence?

Not by itself. The exception requires that the imputation of truth be made for the public good, and that is a question of fact for the court.

Can I be prosecuted for a social media post?

Yes, if the post contains a defamatory imputation published to others. Posts, comments, reels and forwarded messages can all be examined.

Can I claim compensation for defamation?

Yes, by filing a civil suit for damages and an injunction. This is separate from the criminal complaint.

This article is general legal information and not a substitute for advice on your specific case. Consult an advocate before acting.

items.title: Plea Bargaining under BNSS: Eligibility and Process
items.seoTitle: Plea Bargaining under BNSS: Eligibility and Process
items.description: Plea bargaining under BNSS Sections 289 to 300: eligible offences, 30-day rule, victim compensation, reduced sentence limits, appeal bar and when to choose it.
items.html:
Plea bargaining under BNSS lets an accused person plead guilty in return for a lighter sentence, which saves the time and cost of a full trial. The procedure is contained in Chapter XXIII (Sections 289 to 300) of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, and it continues the scheme introduced in the old Code of Criminal Procedure in 2006. This guide explains who can use it, how it works and the risks.

What is plea bargaining under BNSS?

In plea bargaining, the accused applies to the court to be tried on a negotiated basis. The accused admits guilt and, with the prosecution and the victim, works out a mutually satisfactory disposition, including compensation. The court then decides on a reduced sentence within the limits fixed by the Sanhita. The Supreme Court upheld the concept in *State of Gujarat v. Natwar Harchandji Thakor* (2005) and described the safeguards.

Which cases are eligible?

Plea bargaining is available for offences that carry imprisonment of seven years or less. It is not available in these situations:

  • Offences punishable with death or life imprisonment, or imprisonment above seven years.
  • Offences that affect the socio-economic condition of the country, as notified by the Central Government.
  • Offences committed against a woman, or against a child below fourteen years.
  • Cases where the accused has been previously convicted of the same offence.
  • Proceedings involving juveniles under the Juvenile Justice Act.

Time limit for the application

Under the BNSS, the application must be filed within thirty days from the date of framing of charge. This is an important change, since a missed deadline can close the option. The old Code did not impose such a time limit in the same way.

Step-by-step process

  • Application: The accused files an application with a sworn affidavit that the plea is voluntary, that he understands the nature and extent of punishment, and that he has no previous conviction for the offence.
  • Notice: The court issues notice to the Public Prosecutor, the investigating officer, the complainant or victim, and the accused. The victim must be given a chance to participate.
  • Examination in camera: The court examines the accused in private to be satisfied that the plea is voluntary. If it finds the application involuntary, it can proceed with the trial.
  • Mutually satisfactory disposition: The court gives the parties time, up to sixty days, to work out a settlement that includes compensation and other expenses.
  • Report: The agreed disposition is recorded in a report signed by the presiding officer and the participants.
  • Compensation and sentence: The court first awards the agreed compensation to the victim and then hears the parties on punishment.
  • Judgment: The court delivers judgment in open court.

Limits on sentence

The court may sentence the accused to less than the prescribed punishment, subject to ceilings:

  • Where the offence has a minimum sentence, the court may impose up to one-half of it, and up to one-fourth for a first-time offender.
  • Where there is no minimum sentence, the court may impose up to one-fourth of the punishment, and up to one-sixth for a first-time offender.
  • The court may also consider release on probation or admonition where the law permits.

The time already spent in custody is set off against the sentence. Statements made in the plea application cannot be used for any other purpose.

Finality of the judgment

A judgment in a plea bargaining case is final. No ordinary appeal lies, and only a special leave petition to the Supreme Court or a writ petition to the High Court is possible. This finality is the main reason the decision to plead guilty must be taken carefully.

When does it make sense?

  • The evidence against the accused is strong, and conviction is likely.
  • The case is small or medium in gravity and a long trial would cost more than the benefit.
  • A quick closure matters, for example for employment, travel or business reasons.
  • The accused has already spent significant time in custody.

It is a poor choice where the prosecution case is weak or where a conviction would cause serious collateral consequences, such as loss of a licence or profession. Remember that plea bargaining has the effect of a conviction. For other ways to end proceedings, see our guides on quashing of FIR under BNSS Section 528 and criminal appeal and revision under BNSS. The Sanhita is available on India Code.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is plea bargaining under BNSS?

It is a procedure in Chapter XXIII of the Sanhita under which an accused pleads guilty in return for a negotiated, reduced punishment, after agreeing compensation with the victim.

Which sections of the BNSS deal with it?

Sections 289 to 300. Section 290 deals with the application, and Section 293 with the sentencing limits and compensation.

Can anyone accused of an offence apply?

No. The offence must carry imprisonment of seven years or less. Offences against women or children below fourteen, and offences affecting the socio-economic condition of the country, are excluded.

What is the time limit to apply?

The application must be made within thirty days from the date of framing of charge. After that, the option is generally lost.

Can I appeal after a plea bargaining judgment?

No ordinary appeal lies. Only a special leave petition to the Supreme Court or a writ petition to the High Court is available, so the decision should be made with full legal advice.

Does the victim have a say?

Yes. The victim must be given notice and a chance to take part in settling the disposition, and the court first awards the agreed compensation.

Does plea bargaining count as a conviction?

Yes. The judgment is a conviction, and it may have consequences for jobs, licences and visas. Consider these before applying.

This article is general legal information and not a substitute for advice on your specific case. Consult an advocate before acting.

items.title: Maintenance under Section 144 BNSS: Who Can Claim
items.seoTitle: Maintenance under Section 144 BNSS: Who Can Claim
items.description: Maintenance under Section 144 BNSS (old Section 125 CrPC): who can claim, 60-day interim maintenance, how it is fixed, enforcement and key rulings.
items.html:
Maintenance under Section 144 BNSS is a quick, summary remedy that lets a wife, child or parent claim monthly support from a person who has the means but neglects or refuses to provide it. It replaces Section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and applies to people of all religions. This guide explains who can claim, how the amount is decided, how the order is enforced and what the Supreme Court has said.

Who can claim maintenance under Section 144 BNSS?

A Magistrate of the first class can order a person who has sufficient means, but neglects or refuses to maintain, to pay a monthly allowance to:

  • His wife, who is unable to maintain herself. The term includes a divorced woman who has not remarried.
  • His legitimate or illegitimate minor child, whether married or not, who is unable to maintain itself.
  • His adult child, married or unmarried, who has a physical or mental abnormality or injury and cannot maintain itself.
  • His father or mother, who is unable to maintain himself or herself.

There is no upper limit on the amount. The old cap of five hundred rupees was removed years ago, and the court fixes a reasonable sum.

Interim maintenance

The Magistrate can order interim maintenance while the case is pending. The law requires that an application for interim maintenance be disposed of, as far as possible, within 60 days from the date of service of notice on the other side. The final application is meant to be a summary proceeding and not a long trial.

How is the amount decided?

There is no formula, but courts consider:

  • The income, assets and liabilities of both spouses.
  • The standard of living during the marriage.
  • The needs of the wife and children, including education and medical needs.
  • The earning capacity of the wife and whether she was forced to give up work.
  • The age and health of the parties and the responsibilities of the husband.

In *Rajnesh v. Neha* (2020), the Supreme Court directed both parties to file a detailed affidavit of assets and liabilities. It also said maintenance should ordinarily be awarded from the date of the application and that overlapping claims under different laws must be disclosed and adjusted so that the same amount is not paid twice.

When can a wife be refused maintenance?

Under the Section, a wife is not entitled to an allowance if she is living in adultery, if she refuses without sufficient reason to live with her husband, or if they are living separately by mutual consent. These are matters of evidence and are decided by the court after hearing both sides.

Muslim women and Section 144

In *Mohd. Abdul Samad v. State of Telangana* (2024), the Supreme Court held that a divorced Muslim woman can claim maintenance under Section 125 CrPC, now Section 144 BNSS, irrespective of personal law. The provision is secular and applies to all married women.

Where to file and what to attach

The application can be filed before the Magistrate (or the Family Court, where one is functioning) of the district where the husband or wife resides, where the person against whom it is made resides, or where they last lived together. A good application includes:

  • Marriage proof, birth certificates of children and ID proofs.
  • Proof of the husband's income: salary slips, business records, bank statements and tax returns.
  • Records of expenses: school fees, rent, medical bills.
  • The affidavit of assets and liabilities as required by the Supreme Court.

Enforcement of the order

If the person does not pay, the Magistrate can issue a warrant to recover the arrears as if it were a fine. He can also sentence the defaulter to imprisonment for up to one month for each month's default (or until payment, if earlier). An application for enforcement should be made within one year of the date the amount fell due.

Other routes for maintenance

Section 144 is not the only remedy. Maintenance can also be claimed under:

  • The Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956.
  • Sections 24 and 25 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, in divorce and related cases.
  • The Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005.

Courts take earlier awards into account to avoid double payment. If criminal proceedings between the spouses are also pending, read our guide on cruelty and dowry harassment under BNS Section 85. You can read the Sanhita on India Code.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Section 144 BNSS?

It is the maintenance provision of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita. It replaces Section 125 CrPC and lets a wife, child or parent claim monthly maintenance from a person who neglects or refuses to support them despite having the means.

Is there a maximum amount of maintenance?

No. The Magistrate fixes a reasonable amount based on the means and needs of the parties. There is no statutory ceiling.

How quickly is interim maintenance decided?

The law requires an application for interim maintenance to be disposed of within 60 days of service of notice on the other party, as far as possible.

Can a working wife claim maintenance?

Yes, if her income is not enough to maintain herself in a manner reasonably consistent with the standard of living in the marriage. The court looks at her actual income and needs.

Can a divorced wife claim under Section 144?

Yes, as long as she has not remarried and is unable to maintain herself. The right applies to women of all religions.

What happens if the husband does not pay?

The Magistrate can recover the arrears like a fine and can send him to prison for up to one month for each month of default. The application for recovery should be made within one year of the due date.

Can parents claim maintenance from their children?

Yes. A father or mother who cannot maintain himself or herself can claim monthly maintenance from a son or daughter who has sufficient means.

This article is general legal information and not a substitute for advice on your specific case. Consult an advocate before acting.

items.title: Cruelty and Dowry Harassment under BNS Section 85
items.seoTitle: Cruelty and Dowry Harassment under BNS Section 85
items.description: Cruelty and dowry harassment under BNS Sections 85 and 86 (old 498A): meaning, punishment, Dowry Act, arrest limits, false-case safeguards and remedies.
items.html:
Cruelty and dowry harassment by a husband or his relatives is an offence under Section 85 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS), which replaced Section 498A of the Indian Penal Code. The law protects married women from cruelty, but the Supreme Court has also warned against its misuse. This guide explains what the offence is, what the punishment is, and what both complainants and accused persons should do.

Cruelty and dowry harassment: what does BNS Section 85 provide?

Section 85 punishes a husband or a relative of the husband who subjects a woman to cruelty. The punishment is imprisonment up to three years and a fine. The offence is cognizable and non-bailable, and it is triable by a Magistrate.

What is cruelty under Section 86?

Section 86 defines cruelty in two limbs:

  • Wilful conduct that is likely to drive the woman to commit suicide or to cause grave injury or danger to her life, limb or health, whether mental or physical.
  • Harassment of the woman with a view to coercing her or any person related to her to meet an unlawful demand for property or valuable security, or harassment because of her or her relatives' failure to meet such a demand.

Not every quarrel in a marriage is cruelty. The conduct must be serious and wilful, and it must fall within one of these limbs.

Dowry-related laws

Dowry harassment is addressed by more than one law:

  • Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961: Giving, taking or abetting dowry is punishable under Section 3, and demanding dowry is punishable under Section 4.
  • Dowry death (BNS Section 80): If a woman dies within seven years of marriage in unnatural circumstances and she was subjected to cruelty or dowry harassment soon before death, the husband or relatives can be charged. The law raises a presumption against them in such cases.
  • Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005: A civil remedy that provides protection orders, residence rights and monetary relief without requiring a criminal trial.

Who can complain and how

The woman herself, or her blood relatives or relatives by marriage, can complain to the police. The FIR is registered under Section 173 BNSS. If the police do not register it, the complaint can be sent to the Superintendent of Police or taken to the Magistrate. You can read more in our guide on FIR registration under BNSS Section 173.

A strong complaint states dates, places, specific acts and demands, and it is supported by messages, call records, medical records, bank transfers and the names of witnesses.

Safeguards for accused persons

The Supreme Court has repeatedly cautioned against casual arrests and the roping in of distant relatives.

  • Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar (2014): The police must not arrest automatically in offences punishable up to seven years. They must record reasons and issue a notice of appearance instead where arrest is not necessary. The notice procedure now sits in Section 35 BNSS.
  • Preeti Gupta v. State of Jharkhand (2010) and later rulings have noted a tendency to exaggerate allegations and implicate the whole family.
  • In recent decisions, such as *Achin Gupta v. State of Haryana* (2024) and *Dara Lakshmi Narayana v. State of Telangana* (2024), the Supreme Court has quashed proceedings where allegations against relatives were vague, general and omnibus.

For arrest rights, see our guide on arrest and detention rights under BNSS. If arrest is feared, anticipatory bail under BNSS Section 482 is the usual remedy. Where the case is plainly an abuse of process or the parties settle, a petition for quashing of FIR under BNSS Section 528 may be considered.

Practical advice for the complainant

  • Preserve evidence from the beginning: messages, photographs, medical reports and receipts.
  • Seek medical examination and record injuries.
  • Ask for the Domestic Violence Act remedies and maintenance alongside the criminal complaint where needed.
  • Be specific and truthful. Exaggeration weakens an otherwise genuine case.

Practical advice for the accused

  • Do not ignore police notices. Attend and cooperate, with a lawyer's advice.
  • Gather proof of the real situation: chats, travel records, proof of residence of the relatives, and bank records that contradict the allegations.
  • Consider mediation or settlement if appropriate, since the court can quash proceedings on genuine settlement in suitable matrimonial cases.

The Dowry Prohibition Act and the Sanhita can be read on India Code.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the new section for 498A?

Section 85 of the BNS, read with the definition of cruelty in Section 86. The punishment is imprisonment up to three years and a fine.

Is cruelty under Section 85 a bailable offence?

No. It is cognizable and non-bailable. In practice, courts often grant bail or anticipatory bail, and the police are expected to follow the Arnesh Kumar guidelines before arrest.

Can the husband's relatives be arrested automatically?

No. The police must record reasons and consider issuing a notice of appearance. Courts have quashed cases where distant relatives were implicated through vague allegations.

Can the case be settled?

The offence is not compoundable as of right, but the High Court can quash the proceedings on a genuine settlement in appropriate cases.

What is the difference between Section 85 and the Domestic Violence Act?

Section 85 is a criminal offence leading to trial and punishment. The Domestic Violence Act is a civil law that gives protection orders, residence and monetary relief.

Is there a time limit for filing the complaint?

There is a general limitation for taking cognizance of offences punishable up to three years, but courts have flexibility in continuing offences and may condone delay. Delay can weaken the case, so act early.

What if the allegations are false?

The accused can seek quashing of the FIR, discharge, or acquittal, and can take other lawful action. A false complaint can itself lead to legal consequences.

This article is general legal information and not a substitute for advice on your specific case. Consult an advocate before acting.

items.title: Regular Bail and Default Bail under BNSS: Rules, Process
items.seoTitle: Regular Bail and Default Bail under BNSS: Rules, Process
items.description: Regular bail and default bail under BNSS: bailable and non-bailable offences, Sections 478, 480, 483, 187 and 479, 60/90-day rule, conditions and cancellation.
items.html:
Regular bail and default bail are the two most common ways an accused person secures release from custody. Regular bail depends on the court's assessment of the case, while default bail is a right that arises when the police fail to complete the investigation in time. Both are now governed by the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS), which replaced the Code of Criminal Procedure. This guide explains how each works, the sections involved and the practical steps.

Bailable and non-bailable offences

The first question is whether the offence is bailable. The First Schedule of the Sanhita classifies every offence.

  • Bailable offence (Section 478 BNSS): Bail is a matter of right. The police or the court must release the accused on furnishing a bond, with or without sureties.
  • Non-bailable offence (Section 480 BNSS): Bail is a matter of discretion. The court looks at the nature and gravity of the offence, the likelihood of absconding or tampering with witnesses, the accused's antecedents and the stage of the case.
  • A person accused of an offence punishable with death or life imprisonment is not ordinarily released if there are reasonable grounds to believe he is guilty. The law makes exceptions for women, children, and sick or infirm persons.

Regular bail and default bail: how regular bail works

Regular bail is sought after arrest. The application goes first to the Magistrate. For serious offences triable by the Court of Session, or after a Magistrate refuses bail, the application goes to the Sessions Court or the High Court under Section 483 BNSS.

Courts apply well-settled principles. The Supreme Court has said repeatedly that bail is the rule and jail the exception, and that pre-trial detention should not be a punishment. In *Satender Kumar Antil v. CBI* (2022), the Court asked investigating agencies and courts to avoid needless arrests and to treat bail applications with a clear framework of categories of offences.

Factors usually weighed:

  • The seriousness of the allegation and the punishment prescribed.
  • Prima facie material against the accused.
  • Risk of flight, tampering with evidence or influencing witnesses.
  • The accused's criminal history, age, health and family ties.
  • Time already spent in custody and the likely time for trial.

Courts may impose conditions: surrender of passport, reporting to the police station, not leaving the city, and not contacting witnesses. Conditions must be reasonable and connected to the purpose of bail.

What is default bail under Section 187 BNSS?

Default bail, also called statutory bail, arises when the police do not file the final report (charge sheet) within the period allowed after the first remand.

  • 60 days where the offence is punishable with imprisonment of less than ten years.
  • 90 days where the offence is punishable with death, life imprisonment or imprisonment of ten years or more.

If the charge sheet is not filed in time, the accused has an indefeasible right to be released on bail, provided he applies and is ready to furnish bond. The right is lost once the charge sheet is filed before the application is made. An incomplete charge sheet filed only to defeat the right does not stop the clock, according to Supreme Court rulings.

Two points need attention:

  • The BNSS says "ten years or more", whereas the old Code said "not less than ten years". High Courts have read the phrase differently for offences with a maximum of ten years, and the question is still unsettled. Claim the earlier date and be ready to argue the classification.
  • Under Section 187(2), police custody of up to 15 days can now be taken in parts, but it must be sought within the first 40 or 60 days. This does not extend the default bail period.

Special laws such as the NDPS Act and UAPA have their own longer periods.

Release of undertrial prisoners: Section 479 BNSS

Section 479 gives relief to persons who have spent long periods in custody awaiting trial. An undertrial who has served half the maximum sentence for the offence is entitled to be released on bond. A first-time offender becomes eligible after one-third of the maximum sentence. The section does not apply to offences punishable with death or life imprisonment, and the jail authorities must move the court when the person becomes eligible. Time lost because of the accused's own delay is not counted.

Step-by-step procedure

  • Collect the FIR, remand order, arrest memo and the case diary details your lawyer can obtain.
  • Prepare the bail application with grounds, personal details, residence proof and surety documents.
  • Ask for notice to the Public Prosecutor and, where required, the complainant or victim.
  • Argue the application. If it is dismissed, file before the higher court.
  • On release, furnish the bond and sureties and follow every condition strictly.

If arrest has not yet happened, consider anticipatory bail under BNSS Section 482. Knowing your rights at the time of arrest also matters, as explained in our guide on arrest and detention rights under BNSS.

Cancellation of bail

The prosecution or the complainant can ask the court to cancel bail if the accused violates a condition, threatens witnesses, commits a fresh offence or misuses liberty. The High Court and the Sessions Court can also set aside an order granting bail if it was passed without considering relevant material. The text of the Sanhita is available on India Code.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the difference between regular bail and default bail?

Regular bail is granted at the court's discretion after weighing the facts of the case. Default bail is a statutory right that arises when the investigation is not completed and the charge sheet is not filed within 60 or 90 days.

Which sections of the BNSS deal with bail?

Section 478 covers bailable offences, Section 480 non-bailable offences, Section 482 anticipatory bail, Section 483 the special powers of the High Court and the Sessions Court, Section 187 default bail, and Section 479 release of long-term undertrial prisoners.

Can default bail be refused if the charge sheet is filed after my application?

Not if you applied after the period expired and before the charge sheet was filed, and you were ready to furnish bail. Courts have held that filing the application on expiry is enough, even if the court decides it later.

Is there a fixed amount for bail bond?

No. The court fixes a reasonable amount having regard to the offence and the accused's means. An excessive bond amount can defeat the purpose of bail.

What happens if I break a bail condition?

The prosecution can apply for cancellation, and the court may send you back to custody. Compliance with every condition, including reporting dates, is essential.

Can the High Court grant bail directly?

Yes, under Section 483 BNSS the High Court has wide powers. In practice, the usual route is to approach the Magistrate or Sessions Court first, unless there is a special reason.

Do I need a lawyer for a bail application?

A well-drafted application with correct sections, case law and documents greatly improves the chance of success, so legal assistance is strongly advised.

This article is general legal information and not a substitute for advice on your specific case. Consult an advocate before acting.

items.title: Cybercrime and Online Fraud: BNS, IT Act and Reporting
items.seoTitle: Cybercrime and Online Fraud: BNS, IT Act and Reporting
items.description: Cybercrime and online fraud in India: IT Act Sections 66C and 66D, BNS cheating, how to report on 1930, evidence rules and defence for accused.
items.html:
Cybercrime and online fraud are growing fast, from UPI scams and fake investment apps to phishing and digital arrest threats. Both victims and accused need to understand the law. This guide explains the offences under the Information Technology Act, 2000 and the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS), how to report, and how to defend.

Main offences in cybercrime and online fraud

Under the IT Act, 2000:

  • Section 66: Computer-related offences, such as hacking and unauthorised access, if done dishonestly or fraudulently.
  • Section 66C: Identity theft, which is fraudulent or dishonest use of another person's password, electronic signature or unique identification feature.
  • Section 66D: Cheating by personation using a computer resource or communication device.
  • Section 66E: Violation of privacy by capturing or sharing private images.
  • Sections 67 and 67A: Publishing obscene or sexually explicit material electronically.

Under the BNS:

  • Section 318: Cheating.
  • Section 319: Cheating by personation.
  • Section 336: Forgery, including electronic records.
  • Section 351: Criminal intimidation.
  • Other provisions for extortion, stalking and defamation may also apply.

For the ingredients of cheating, read our guide on cheating and criminal breach of trust under BNS.

Common types of online fraud

  • Phishing links and fake bank calls to steal OTPs.
  • UPI and QR code frauds.
  • Fake investment, trading and job schemes.
  • SIM swap and identity theft.
  • Fake customer care numbers and remote access apps.
  • Sextortion and morphed images.
  • Calls threatening arrest by impersonating officials, often called digital arrest.

How to report: act in the first hours

  • Call the national cybercrime helpline 1930 quickly in a financial fraud, because early reporting helps in freezing the money.
  • File a complaint on the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal (cybercrime.gov.in).
  • Inform your bank immediately and ask them to block the card or account and note the complaint number.
  • Lodge a complaint at the local police or cyber crime police station. For how an FIR is registered, see FIR registration under BNSS Section 173.

Banks are expected to follow the RBI framework on customer liability for unauthorised electronic transactions, where timely reporting by the customer limits the customer's liability. Check the current circular with your bank.

Preserve digital evidence

  • Take screenshots of chats, links, call logs and transaction messages.
  • Save emails with full headers, and keep the original device.
  • Note UPI reference numbers, account numbers, and dates and times.
  • Do not delete messages or reset the phone.

Electronic evidence in court

The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA) treats electronic records as documents. Section 63 BSA, which corresponds to the old Section 65B of the Evidence Act, requires a certificate for producing electronic records as evidence, in the form prescribed by the Act. The certificate is generally given by the person in charge of the device and an expert, and incorrect or missing certificates can weaken a case.

If you are accused: key defence points

  • Mistaken identity or mule accounts: Many people are drawn in when their bank account is used to receive money from fraud. Show the lack of knowledge and intention.
  • No dishonest intention: Show that you were an innocent intermediary.
  • Weak electronic evidence: Challenge the certificate, chain of custody and integrity of the data.
  • Account freeze: If your account is frozen on a complaint, you can apply to the Magistrate or the High Court for release or de-freezing, with proof of the source of funds.
  • Protection from arrest: Consider anticipatory bail under BNSS Section 482, and know your arrest rights under BNSS.

Civil remedies for victims

Along with the criminal case, the victim can pursue the bank or intermediary for liability where the law permits, ask for blocking of fraudulent accounts and websites, and in some cases seek compensation through adjudication under the IT Act.

Frequently Asked Questions

What number should I call to report online financial fraud?

The national cybercrime helpline is 1930. Report it as early as possible and also file a complaint on cybercrime.gov.in and with your bank.

Which IT Act sections apply to identity theft and impersonation fraud?

Section 66C deals with identity theft and Section 66D deals with cheating by personation using a computer resource, along with BNS provisions on cheating and personation.

Is hacking a crime in India?

Yes. Unauthorised access done dishonestly or fraudulently is punishable under Section 66 of the IT Act, read with Section 43, along with other applicable laws.

Can I get my money back after a UPI fraud?

Sometimes. Quick reporting helps in freezing the amount, and the bank's liability depends on the facts and the RBI rules on unauthorised transactions. Delay reduces the chances.

Is a screenshot enough as evidence in court?

Screenshots help in the investigation, but for court, electronic records need proper certification under Section 63 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, and the original device or data should be preserved.

My bank account was frozen because of a fraud complaint. What can I do?

Apply to the Magistrate or the High Court for de-freezing, with bank statements and proof showing the source of the funds and your lack of involvement.

What is a digital arrest scam?

It is a fraud where criminals pose as officials on a call and threaten arrest to extort money. No genuine agency arrests anyone by video call, so disconnect and report on 1930.

This article is general legal information and not a substitute for advice on your specific case. Consult an advocate before acting.

items.title: Criminal Appeal and Revision under BNSS: Forums and Process
items.seoTitle: Criminal Appeal and Revision under BNSS: Forums and Process
items.description: Criminal appeal and revision under BNSS: who can appeal, which court, victim's right, suspension of sentence, bail pending appeal and revision powers.
items.html:
A conviction is not the end of the road. The law gives an accused the right to challenge it through an appeal, and gives courts a power of revision to correct errors. This guide explains criminal appeal and revision under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS), which applies to appeals filed on or after 1 July 2024.

Appeal against conviction

Section 413 BNSS states the general rule that no appeal lies except as provided by the Sanhita or another law. Section 415 deals with appeals from convictions:

  • A person convicted by a Magistrate can generally appeal to the Court of Session.
  • A person convicted by a Sessions Judge or Additional Sessions Judge can appeal to the High Court.
  • Appeals in some cases lie directly to the High Court, depending on the sentence and the court that tried the case.
  • A person convicted by the High Court in its original jurisdiction appeals to the Supreme Court as the law provides.

Victim's right to appeal

The proviso to Section 413 gives the victim the right to appeal against an order of acquittal, conviction for a lesser offence, or inadequate compensation. This is an important right, because the victim does not have to wait for the State to act.

Appeal by the State against acquittal

Section 419 allows the State to appeal against an order of acquittal. In many cases, the appeal against acquittal to the High Court requires the leave of the High Court. Appellate courts are slow to interfere with an acquittal, because the presumption of innocence is strengthened by the acquittal.

Suspension of sentence and bail pending appeal

Section 430 BNSS allows the appellate court to suspend the sentence and release the convict on bail while the appeal is pending, recording its reasons. This is crucial because appeals take years. Courts consider:

  • The nature and gravity of the offence and the sentence.
  • Whether the appeal has a good arguable case.
  • The likely delay in hearing the appeal.
  • The convict's conduct during trial, including whether he was on bail.

Where the sentence is for a fixed term, courts are generally more willing to suspend it if the appeal is unlikely to be heard before most of the term is served.

Limitation for filing an appeal

Appeals are subject to the limitation periods in the Limitation Act, 1963. The periods differ according to the court and the type of order, and appeals against acquittal often have a longer period. If you miss the date, you can apply to condone the delay with a proper explanation. Always check the exact limit with your advocate at the time of judgment, and file as early as possible.

Revision: what is it?

Revision is a supervisory power. Higher courts can call for and examine the records of a lower court to check the correctness, legality or propriety of a finding, sentence or order, and the regularity of its proceedings.

  • High Court: Sections 438 and 442 BNSS.
  • Sessions Court: Sections 438, 440 and 441 BNSS, depending on the judge.

Limits on revision

  • Revision is not a second appeal. Courts usually do not re-appreciate evidence in revision.
  • The power should not be used to interfere with interlocutory orders in a routine manner.
  • A revision cannot convert a finding of acquittal into conviction.
  • A person who has a right of appeal should generally use the appeal.

Criminal appeal and revision: key differences

  • Appeal: A statutory right, which allows the court to re-examine facts and law.
  • Revision: A discretionary supervisory remedy, focused on illegality, impropriety and jurisdictional error.
  • Scope: Appeal is wide, revision is narrow.

Other remedies

  • Inherent powers of the High Court: To prevent abuse of process. See our guide on quashing of FIR under BNSS Section 528.
  • Special leave petition: Against High Court orders before the Supreme Court under Article 136.
  • Mercy and remission: As provided by law.

Practical tips

  • Obtain a certified copy of the judgment and the full trial record immediately.
  • Decide quickly whether to appeal, and which sections of the evidence to challenge.
  • Apply for suspension of sentence along with the appeal.
  • Prepare a clear list of grounds, covering law and facts.
  • The Sanhita is available on India Code.

Frequently Asked Questions

Where do I appeal if a Magistrate convicts me?

Generally to the Court of Session, under Section 415 BNSS. The exact forum depends on the court and the sentence, so confirm it with your advocate.

Can a victim appeal against an acquittal?

Yes. The proviso to Section 413 BNSS gives the victim the right to appeal against acquittal, conviction for a lesser offence, or inadequate compensation.

Can I get bail after conviction?

Yes. The appellate court can suspend the sentence and release you on bail under Section 430 BNSS while the appeal is pending, after recording reasons.

What is the difference between appeal and revision?

An appeal is a statutory right that allows re-examination of facts and law. Revision is a supervisory power focused on legality, propriety and jurisdictional errors.

Is there a time limit to appeal?

Yes, under the Limitation Act, and it varies by court and type of order. Delay can be condoned for sufficient cause, but file as early as possible.

Can the State appeal against an acquittal?

Yes, under Section 419 BNSS, usually with the leave of the High Court.

Which BNSS sections deal with revision?

Sections 438 and 442 for the High Court, and Sections 438, 440 and 441 for Sessions Courts.

This article is general legal information and not a substitute for advice on your specific case. Consult an advocate before acting.

items.title: Cheating and Criminal Breach of Trust under BNS: Defences
items.seoTitle: Cheating and Criminal Breach of Trust under BNS: Defences
items.description: Cheating and criminal breach of trust under BNS Sections 318 and 316: ingredients, punishment, civil vs criminal disputes, defences and remedies.
items.html:
Cheating and criminal breach of trust are among the most common charges in business, money and property disputes. Under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS), cheating is in Section 318 and criminal breach of trust is in Section 316. They replace Sections 420 and 406 of the old Indian Penal Code. This guide explains what the prosecution must prove and how an accused can defend.

What is cheating under BNS Section 318?

Cheating means deceiving a person and thereby fraudulently or dishonestly inducing him to deliver property or consent to a person retaining property, or intentionally inducing him to do or omit something that he would not otherwise do, and which causes or is likely to cause damage or harm in body, mind, reputation or property.

Punishment (in general terms):

  • Simple cheating: imprisonment up to three years, or fine, or both.
  • Cheating a person whom the offender knows he is bound to protect: up to five years, or fine, or both.
  • Cheating and dishonestly inducing delivery of property or making or altering a valuable security: up to seven years and fine.

Ingredients of cheating

  • A false representation or deception.
  • The accused had a dishonest or fraudulent intention at the time of making the promise.
  • The victim was induced to deliver property or to act.
  • Loss or harm followed, or was likely.

The most important element is dishonest intention at the beginning. A later failure to keep a promise, without proof of that intention from the start, is a breach of contract and not cheating.

What is criminal breach of trust under Section 316?

A person commits criminal breach of trust when, being entrusted with property or with dominion over property, he dishonestly misappropriates or converts it to his own use, or dishonestly uses or disposes of it in violation of a direction of law or a legal contract.

Punishment (in general terms):

  • General offence: imprisonment up to five years, or fine, or both.
  • By a carrier, wharfinger or warehouse-keeper: up to seven years and fine.
  • By a clerk or servant: up to seven years and fine.
  • By a public servant, banker, merchant, agent, broker or attorney in the course of business: life imprisonment or up to ten years, and fine.

Ingredients of criminal breach of trust

  • Entrustment of property to the accused.
  • Dishonest misappropriation, conversion or disposal of that property.
  • Intention to cause wrongful gain or loss.

Mere failure to pay a debt is not criminal breach of trust, because a debtor is not holding the money as a trustee.

Civil dispute or criminal case?

Courts have repeatedly warned against giving criminal colour to civil disputes. In Indian Oil Corporation v. NEPC India Ltd. (2006), the Supreme Court cautioned about the growing tendency to convert purely civil disputes into criminal cases. In Hridaya Ranjan Prasad Verma v. State of Bihar (2000), the Court explained that the distinction between breach of contract and cheating lies in the intention at the time of making the promise.

The Supreme Court has also observed, for example in Delhi Race Club (1940) Ltd. v. State of U.P. (2024), that cheating and criminal breach of trust involve different mental states and ordinarily do not co-exist in the same transaction. The question must be examined on the facts of each case.

Defences in cheating and criminal breach of trust

  • No dishonest intention at the inception. The dispute is about performance of a contract.
  • No entrustment. The money was a loan or advance, not held in trust.
  • No false representation, or the complainant knew the true facts.
  • No loss or delivery of property.
  • Delay, motive and falsity in the complaint.
  • Payments already made, or a settlement reached.

Remedies for an accused

  • If arrest is feared, consider anticipatory bail under BNSS Section 482.
  • Where the FIR shows only a civil dispute, a petition for quashing of FIR under BNSS Section 528 can be filed.
  • Many of these offences are compoundable, some with the permission of the court, under the compounding table in the BNSS, so a settlement can end the case. Check the table for the exact section.
  • Know how the case began by reading about FIR registration under BNSS Section 173.

Advice for complainants

  • Keep documents showing the promise, the payment and the dishonest act.
  • Give a clear chronology in the complaint.
  • Consider a civil recovery suit at the same time if money is the real goal.
  • Avoid exaggeration, since courts examine the complaint closely.

Frequently Asked Questions

Which BNS sections replace Section 420 and Section 406 of the IPC?

Cheating is dealt with in Section 318 of the BNS, and criminal breach of trust is in Section 316 of the BNS.

Is every failure to repay money a cheating case?

No. A breach of contract or failure to repay becomes cheating only if the prosecution proves that the accused had a dishonest intention from the very beginning.

What must be proved for criminal breach of trust?

The prosecution must show that property was entrusted to the accused, and that he dishonestly misappropriated, converted or disposed of it.

Can the same facts be both a civil suit and a criminal case?

They can be, but courts discourage criminal proceedings that are really civil disputes. Each case depends on whether the ingredients of the offence are made out.

Can cheating cases be settled?

Many are compoundable, some with court permission. The parties can compound the offence and end the case, or approach the High Court for quashing on a genuine settlement.

What is the punishment for criminal breach of trust by a banker or agent?

It is more serious. Under Section 316, it can extend to imprisonment for life or up to ten years, along with a fine.

What should I do if I receive a police notice in a cheating case?

Do not ignore it. Consult an advocate, collect your documents, appear on the date, and consider the protective remedies available before arrest becomes likely.

This article is general legal information and not a substitute for advice on your specific case. Consult an advocate before acting.
